trends:
**What changed between 2025 and 2027**

1. **AI split the loop into AI-off and AI-on rounds.** Live algorithm rounds stay AI-off almost everywhere, and
   interviewers now interrupt with "why this structure?" to check the reasoning is yours. At the same time, Meta
   (since October 2025) replaced one of its two coding rounds with an AI-enabled round, Google is piloting an
   AI-assisted code-comprehension round in 2026, and Canva expects candidates to use AI. Take-homes now come with a live walkthrough.
2. **"Real work" formats grew fast.** Debug-this-code, code review, and practical coding with changing requirements
   and tests are replacing some puzzle rounds. All ten Stripe experiences in one 2026 analysis were practical work.
3. **DSA didn't die. It became the gate.** In the same analysis, LinkedIn (8/8), Google (7/9) and Amazon (6/8)
   still asked classic DSA. In India, Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, Amazon, PhonePe and Goldman Sachs loops in 2025-26 all
   included an OA or a DSA round. Problems are mostly medium, and *explaining* counts as much as solving.
4. **System design moved down to SDE-2.** Flipkart, Uber, Razorpay and Amazon SDE-2 loops in 2025-26 all had a
   high-level design round, with prompts about payments, failures and retries rather than "design Twitter".
5. **Depth rounds decide the level.** Resume and project deep dives, hiring manager rounds and behavioral rounds can
   downlevel a strong coder: Atlassian and Amazon both do it. India's machine-coding round (Flipkart, PhonePe,
   Razorpay, Uber, Swiggy) is still the main filter for SDE-2.
6. **The market got stricter.** Fewer openings and more applicants mean borderline rounds fail more often. With
   offer dropout high, companies probe notice periods and joining intent harder than before.

**What this means for Raj: priorities, in order**

1. **DSA fluency in Java for OAs and live rounds (about 25% of prep time).** Mediums across about 15 patterns,
   solved out loud. Don't grind hards: a few per pattern is enough.
2. **Machine coding plus concurrency (about 20%).** This is the round that separates SDE-2 offers at Indian product
   companies, and a Java developer can get very good at it. Build one system a week, timed, and always answer
   "what if two threads do this?".
3. **System design with failure paths (about 20%).** One design a week. Lead with idempotency, retries,
   consistency and observability, and use stories from your own Spring Boot and MySQL work for depth.
4. **Your own stack, deep (about 15%).** Spring transactions and proxies, JPA fetching, InnoDB indexes and locks,
   Angular change detection. These rounds can't be bluffed, and your two years are an advantage only if you can go
   five "whys" deep.
5. **Stories and HR (about 10%).** Eight to ten stories with numbers, one project brief, and a scripted answer on
   CTC and notice period.
6. **Code review, debugging and AI-assisted coding (about 10%).** Cheap to practise and growing: review one file
   a week out loud, and do one AI-pair session where you verify everything.

**What to skip:** staff-level design topics, exotic technologies you can't defend, LeetCode hards beyond a handful,
and memorising answers you can't explain. Each round below shows how it's scored, a worked example, the common ways
people fail, and exactly what to practise on this site.

rounds.title: Online Assessment (OA)
rounds.summary: A timed, auto-graded coding test (HackerRank, CodeSignal, HackerEarth) that filters you before any engineer sees you. For SDE-2 it is usually two medium to medium-hard problems in 60-120 minutes, scored by hidden test cases.
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 60-120 minutes. Usually 2 coding problems, sometimes 3, plus optional MCQs on Java, SQL, OS or aptitude.
- **Platform:** HackerRank, CodeSignal, HackerEarth or the company's own portal. You run code against sample tests, then submit against hidden tests.
- **Scoring:** automatic and per test case, so a brute force that passes 60% of cases scores more than a clever solution that times out.
- **Proctoring:** tab-switch logs, full-screen mode, blocked paste, sometimes webcam and photo ID, and plagiarism comparison across candidates. **No AI tools.**
- **Variants:**
  - Amazon adds a *work-style simulation*: scenario questions on trade-offs such as quick patch vs proper fix, or latency vs durability.
  - Atlassian uses a live **Karat** screen: about 20 minutes of rapid design questions, then two coding problems with a human watching. A retake within 48 hours was allowed in one 2024 report.
  - CodeSignal's *Industry Coding* format: one project (for example an in-memory store) extended over 4 levels in about 90 minutes.
- **Difficulty in 2025-26 SDE-2 reports:** graph/BFS with a twist and a trie (Flipkart, Jan 2026), DP state transition and constrained shortest path (Amazon, Jul 2025), near-hard BST/deque/graph problems (Uber on CodeSignal).
whatTheyTest: Spotting the pattern behind a disguised medium problem within 5-10 minutes
Choosing a complexity that fits the constraints (n = 10^5 means O(n log n) or better)
Edge cases that hidden tests always contain: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, maximum n, overflow
Java fluency under a timer: collections, comparators, long arithmetic, fast input reading
Splitting time across 2-3 problems to collect partial credit
Integrity: flagged attempts are rejected whatever the score
rounds.rubric:
No engineer reads your code at this stage unless something is flagged. The platform produces a score, and the
recruiter applies a cutoff set for the role. The cutoff rises in hiring drives with many applicants.

| What you submit | Typical SDE-2 outcome |
|---|---|
| Both problems pass every hidden test | Clear pass, often fast-tracked |
| One fully solved, one at 60%+ of tests | Usually passes; borderline in big drives |
| One fully solved, nothing on the other | Coin flip, depends on the cutoff |
| Only partial scores, or timeouts on large tests | Usually rejected |
| Plagiarism, tab-switch or proctoring flags | Rejected regardless of score |

**What silently costs points:** Time Limit Exceeded on the big cases (wrong complexity), `int` overflow in sums or
counts, wrong output format, and code that only handles the sample. If you clear the OA, the next interviewer may
open your submission and ask you to explain it, so write code you can defend.
rounds.howToAce:
**Before the test**

1. Do one practice test on the real platform (HackerRank and CodeSignal both have free practice areas) so the editor, input reading and the Run vs Submit buttons hold no surprises.
2. Keep a Java toolkit in your head: `long` for sums and counts, `ArrayDeque` instead of `Stack`, `PriorityQueue` with `Integer.compare` comparators, `HashMap.merge` for counting, `BufferedReader` when input is large.
3. Take the test when you are sharpest, on a stable connection, with notifications off. Invites usually stay open 3-7 days, so warm up with one timed medium that morning.

**During the test**

1. **Read every problem first (3-4 minutes)** and start with the one you recognise. All points count the same.
2. **Read the constraints before you think about the algorithm.** They tell you the target complexity:

| n up to | Aim for |
|---|---|
| 20 | O(2^n), backtracking |
| 500 | O(n^3) |
| 5,000 | O(n^2) |
| 10^5 to 10^6 | O(n log n) or O(n) |
| 10^9 and above | O(log n) or a formula |

3. **Bank partial credit.** If the optimal idea hasn't come after about 10 minutes, submit a correct brute force, note the score, then optimise.
4. **Run your own edge cases before every submit:** empty or size-1 input, all-equal values, negatives, the maximum n, and an answer that needs `long`.
5. **Timebox.** Split the time evenly. When a problem stalls, move on and come back with fresh eyes.
6. **Stay inside the test window.** No tab switching, no pasting from outside. A flag costs more than a missed problem.

**After the test**

Write both problems down from memory and solve them properly within 24 hours. Rounds are often scheduled within a
week, and interviewers sometimes open with "walk me through your OA solution".

**Weekly practice on SwitchPrep**

Three times a week, solve two unseen mediums from the DSA section in 70 minutes with a timer and no hints. Once a
week, take a full Final Round mock day. Log which patterns cost you the most time and revise those notes instead of
starting new topics.
rounds.walkthrough:
**The problem (paraphrased OA style):** A warehouse records a net stock change for every hour: positive for
inbound, negative for dispatch. Count the contiguous stretches of hours whose net change is exactly `k`.
Constraints: `n <= 2 * 10^5`, each value between `-10^4` and `10^4`.

**Minute 0-3: read the constraints first.** n = 2 * 10^5 rules out O(n^2), which would be about 2 * 10^10
operations. The target is O(n) or O(n log n). Values can be **negative**, which is the trap: a sliding window only
works when growing the window can only increase the sum. With negatives, shrinking from the left can raise the sum
too, so the window logic breaks.

**Minute 3-8: bank points.** The strong candidate writes the obvious double loop first, runs the samples and
submits. It passes 7 of 15 tests and times out on the rest. Those 7 tests are now banked.

**Minute 8-15: the real idea.** Let `prefix[i]` be the sum of the first i hours. The stretch from hour j to hour
i-1 sums to `prefix[i] - prefix[j]`, so we need the number of earlier prefixes equal to `prefix[i] - k`. That is
one HashMap lookup per hour:

```java
static long countStretches(int[] change, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    seen.put(0L, 1);                 // empty prefix: a stretch may start at hour 0
    long prefix = 0, count = 0;
    for (int c : change) {
        prefix += c;
        count += seen.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);
        seen.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return count;
}
```

**Minute 15-20: edge cases before submitting.** The candidate checks three things on paper:

- `k = 0` with input `[0, 0, 0]`: the answer is 6 (three single hours, two pairs, one triple). The `seen.put(0L, 1)` seed is what makes the stretches that start at hour 0 count.
- **Overflow:** the count can reach n(n+1)/2, which is about 2 * 10^10 and does not fit in an `int`. Hence `long count`. The prefix itself is bounded by 2 * 10^9, uncomfortably close to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, so it is a `long` too.
- A single hour equal to k, and an input where no stretch matches (answer 0).

Submit: 15/15. Total time is about 20 minutes, which leaves 50+ minutes for the second problem.

**Three days later, the first live round opens like this:**

> **Interviewer:** I see your OA. Walk me through the second problem.
>
> **Candidate:** Brute force was O(n^2) over all start and end pairs, which is too slow for 2 * 10^5. I didn't use a sliding window because the values can be negative, so the window sum isn't monotonic. Instead I count, for each prefix sum, how many earlier prefixes equal `prefix - k`. That's O(n) time and O(n) space for the map.
>
> **Interviewer:** What if I asked for the *longest* such stretch instead of the count?
>
> **Candidate:** Then I'd store the *first* index where each prefix value appears, never overwriting it, and at each hour compute `i - firstIndex[prefix - k]`. Same complexity.

**Why this earns points:** the constraints decided the algorithm before any code was written. Partial credit was
banked early. The negative-values trap was named, not discovered by failing tests. Overflow was handled on
purpose. And because the candidate understood the solution, the OA turned into an easy first five minutes of the
next round instead of an awkward one.
commonFailures: Spending 50 minutes on the first problem and never reading the second
Passing the samples but failing hidden tests through int overflow, empty input or off-by-one
An O(n^2) solution on n = 10^5 because the constraints were never read
Using sliding window on arrays that contain negative numbers
Submitting nothing on a hard problem instead of a brute force that scores partial points
Switching tabs or pasting code, which triggers a proctoring flag and an automatic reject
Taking the test in an unfamiliar language or editor for the first time

rounds.title: DSA Live Coding (AI off, explain as you go)
rounds.summary: 45-60 minutes of live problem solving with an engineer, no AI, where you must think out loud. It is still in almost every loop, but you are judged on how you reason and communicate as much as on the final code.
rounds.weight: ~15-25% of the SDE-2 decision; a clear fail usually vetoes the loop
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 45-60 minutes, one or two problems (medium, sometimes medium-hard), often with a follow-up extension ("now also print every operation").
- **Setup:** a shared editor (CoderPad, HackerRank CodePair, an internal tool). Some have no run button, so you dry-run by hand. Offline drives (Flipkart, Jan 2026) can mean pseudocode on a whiteboard.
- **Rules:** AI off, often no autocomplete. Expect interruptions such as "why a deque here?" or "what's the invariant?" because interviewers now check that the reasoning is yours.
- **Where it sits:** 1-2 rounds per loop. Amazon pairs each coding round with two Leadership Principle questions, and the Bar Raiser round can include a coding problem as well.
whatTheyTest: Clarifying the problem: inputs, constraints, edge cases, a worked example
Moving from a brute force to an optimal approach, with the reason each step is faster
Clean, correct Java: sensible names, small helpers, the right collections
Testing your own code by dry run before the interviewer finds the bug
Accurate time and space complexity, plus how it changes under a follow-up
Talking while thinking, and taking a hint without getting defensive
rounds.rubric:
Most companies score four dimensions independently and then combine them. Rough calibration for SDE-2:

| Dimension | Strong hire | Hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem solving | Finds the optimal approach on their own and explains *why* it works | Reaches the optimum with one small hint | Needs repeated hints or stays at brute force |
| Coding | Idiomatic, bug-light, readable, finished with time to spare | Working, minor bugs fixed when pointed out | Messy, unfinished, or language struggles |
| Verification | Dry-runs, finds own bugs, lists edge cases unprompted | Tests when asked | No testing; the interviewer finds the bugs |
| Communication | Narrates intent, invites feedback, answers follow-ups crisply | Mostly clear with some silent stretches | Long silences, can't explain own code |

A finished optimal solution delivered in silence often scores lower than a slightly slower one where the
interviewer could follow every decision. Working code with no tests or edge-case reasoning can still be marked
"lean no hire" in 2026 rubrics.
rounds.howToAce:
**A 45-minute script you rehearse until it is automatic**

1. **0-5 min, clarify.** Restate the problem in your own words. Ask about input size, value ranges, duplicates, empty input, and what to return when there is no answer. Write one small example and its expected output in the editor.
2. **5-12 min, approach.** Say the brute force and its complexity in one sentence. Then name the bottleneck ("we recompute the window sum each time") and the structure that removes it. Get a nod before coding: "Does that sound reasonable, or should I go straight for X?"
3. **12-32 min, code.** Narrate *intent*, not keystrokes: "Now I'm expanding the frontier one level at a time." Write helper methods for the noisy parts (bounds checks, neighbour generation). Use real names.
4. **32-40 min, test.** Dry-run your example line by line, tracking variables in a comment. Then run 2-3 edge cases out loud. When you find a bug, say what was wrong before you fix it.
5. **40-45 min, wrap up.** State time and space complexity, then pre-empt the follow-up: "If the grid were huge and sparse, I'd store only the active cells."

**Patterns that cover most SDE-2 problems in Indian product-company loops**

Hashing and prefix sums, two pointers, sliding window, binary search on the answer, BFS/DFS on grids and graphs
(multi-source BFS, topological sort), heaps and top-k, intervals, tree recursion (LCA, path sums, level order),
1D/2D DP basics, union-find and tries. Depth on these beats a scattering of hard problems.

**When you are stuck**

Say so, and show your search: "I'm looking for a way to avoid re-scanning; I've ruled out sorting because we need
original indices." Try a smaller input, a different data structure, or reversing the direction of the problem.
Interviewers give hints to people who show their thinking.

**Java habits interviewers notice**

`ArrayDeque` instead of `Stack`, `Integer.compare` in comparators (never `a - b`, which can overflow), `equals`
for boxed `Integer`, `getOrDefault` and `merge` for counting, and marking a cell as visited when you *enqueue*
it, not when you dequeue it.

**How to practise**

Solve out loud, always, even alone. Record one session a week and listen for silences longer than 30 seconds. Do
one mock with a friend every week from the second month on. Mocks are where explain-as-you-go becomes natural.
commonFailures: Coding in silence for 15 minutes, then presenting the result
Jumping into code without a worked example or any clarifying questions
Reproducing a memorised solution but not being able to say why it is correct
Never stating the brute force, so the interviewer can't credit the optimisation
No dry run: the interviewer finds the off-by-one you would have caught
Arguing with a hint, or ignoring it and carrying on down the wrong path
Java slips: `Stack`, `==` on boxed Integers, `a - b` comparators, int overflow
Polishing an optimal idea for 30 minutes instead of first finishing a working one

rounds.title: AI-Assisted Coding
rounds.summary: A newer round where an AI assistant sits inside the editor next to a multi-file codebase you didn't write. You are scored on how you understand, direct and verify the work, not on typing speed.
rounds.weight: Replaces one of the two coding rounds at Meta (~20-25% of that loop)
rounds.format:
- **Meta (since October 2025, up to E7):** about 60 minutes in a three-panel CoderPad: file explorer, editor, and an AI chat that can see the files but only answers in chat. You paste or type the code yourself. Several models are offered (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama variants). Java is supported. Three phases on one problem: **fix a bug → implement the core feature → optimise** for larger hidden test data.
- **Google (2026 pilot, junior and mid-level, select US teams):** a *code comprehension* round with Gemini: read, debug and extend an existing codebase. Described internally as "human-led, AI-assisted".
- **Canva:** an AI-assisted round replaced the CS-fundamentals screen for backend and frontend roles, with deliberately ambiguous, realistic problems that one prompt can't solve.
- **Take-homes:** AI use is often expected, followed by a live walkthrough where you must explain and change your own code.
- **India in 2026:** rare in Indian product-company loops so far. Expect it at global companies' India offices and at AI-first startups. Most Indian loops stay AI-off.
whatTheyTest: Reading an unfamiliar multi-file codebase quickly before touching it
Breaking the task into small, well-specified prompts instead of asking for the whole solution
Verifying every AI output: running tests, checking edge cases and complexity
Catching confident-but-wrong AI code (wrong algorithm, hidden O(n^2), broken invariants)
Owning the result: explaining every line, including lines the AI wrote
Picking the algorithm yourself when larger test data exposes a slow solution
Narrating decisions while juggling the tool and the interviewer
rounds.rubric:
Meta reportedly scores the same four competencies as its classic coding round: problem solving, code quality,
verification and communication. Google's pilot looks for prompt clarity, output validation and debugging. How
those show up with an AI in the room:

| Signal | Strong | Weak |
|---|---|---|
| Orientation | Reads README, models and tests before the first prompt | Prompts "fix the failing test" in minute one |
| Decomposition | Decides the approach, delegates bounded pieces (a helper, boilerplate, test data) | Asks for the full solution and pastes it |
| Prompt quality | Gives types, signatures, constraints, invariants, "don't change X" | Vague one-liners, then several rounds of re-prompting |
| Verification | Runs tests after every change, adds an edge-case test, checks complexity | Trusts the output because it compiles |
| Catching errors | Spots and explains the AI's mistake, fixes it by hand or with a sharper prompt | Doesn't notice until the hidden tests fail |
| Ownership | Explains and simplifies generated code on request | "The AI wrote that part" |

One internal summary quoted by Hello Interview: you *should* use AI, but you must show you understand the code.
Candidates were marked down both for over-reliance and for never using the tool at all.
rounds.howToAce:
**Step by step in the room**

1. **Orient for 5 minutes without AI.** Open the README, the domain classes and the test file. Say what you see: "Three classes. `Allocator` is the entry point, and the tests use a builder for orders." This is where most candidates lose time later.
2. **State your plan before the first prompt.** "I'll fix the failing test, then implement the allocation with a sweep plus a heap, then check against the big dataset."
3. **Bug phase: form the hypothesis yourself.** Read the failing assertion and the code path. Use the AI to confirm or to explain an unfamiliar API, not to find the bug for you. Some candidates report the assistant being deliberately unhelpful in this phase.
4. **Implementation phase: delegate bounded work with rich prompts.** A good prompt has the goal, the signature, the types, the constraints, the invariant and the limits:

> "In `Allocator.java`, write `assign(List<Order>, List<Slot>)` returning `Map<Integer,Integer>` (orderId to slotId). Sort slots by time. Sweep them, pushing orders with `readyAt <= slot.time` into a min-heap by deadline. Discard heap entries whose deadline is before the slot time. Fill up to capacity. Don't modify `Order` or `Slot`. Target O((n+m) log n)."

5. **Review the output like a code review.** Read every line before pasting. Check loop bounds, inclusive or exclusive comparisons, mutation of shared lists, and hidden linear calls inside loops (`removeIf`, `contains` on a list).
6. **Run tests after every paste.** Then ask the AI for edge-case tests, read them, and add your own counterexample for the greedy choice.
7. **Optimisation phase: look at the data first.** Read the size of the large test inputs, compute your complexity, and pick the algorithm yourself. Use the AI to type it.
8. **Narrate throughout.** Before each prompt, say what you're asking for. After it, say what you'll check. Silence while chatting with the model reads as lost control.

**Preparation on SwitchPrep**

- Once a week, take an LLD or practical-coding problem, give yourself 45 minutes with an AI assistant, and follow the steps above. Then close the AI and explain every line out loud.
- Keep solving DSA by hand. The optimisation phase still needs you to recognise BFS, heaps, tries or DP quickly.
- Prepare your answer to "How do you use AI in daily work, and where do you still write code by hand?" It now comes up in behavioral rounds too.
rounds.walkthrough:
**Setup (original example in the Meta/Google style):** a Java repo `slot-allocator` with `Order(id, readyAt,
deadline)`, `Slot(id, time, capacity)`, an `Allocator` class and `AllocatorTest`. Delivery slots leave at a fixed
time. An order can go on any slot whose time falls inside its window (both ends inclusive), and the goal is to
assign as many orders as possible.

**Phase 1: the failing test.**

> **Candidate:** Before I prompt anything, I'll read the models and the test. `Order`'s Javadoc says the window is inclusive on both ends. The failing test is `orderReadyExactlyAtSlotTimeIsEligible`. In `Allocator.isEligible` I see `slot.time() > order.readyAt()`. That's a strict comparison, so an order ready exactly at slot time is rejected. It should be `>=`.
>
> **Interviewer:** You didn't use the AI for that.
>
> **Candidate:** Reading was faster than prompting. I'll change it, run the suite... green. While I was reading I also noticed `assign` sorts the caller's list in place. That's a side effect worth flagging, so I'll copy the list in phase 2.

**Phase 2: implement `assign`.** The candidate first asks the AI for a quick version to see its shape:

> **Prompt:** "Implement `assign` so each order goes into the first eligible slot with capacity left. Return orderId to slotId."
>
> **Candidate (reading the output):** This processes orders in input order and takes the first eligible slot. It compiles, but greedy-by-input-order isn't optimal. Counterexample: order A has window [0,10], order B has [0,1], slot 1 is at t=1 with capacity 1, slot 2 is at t=5 with capacity 1. If A grabs t=1, B gets nothing, so we assign 1. The optimum is 2. I'll write that as a test first.

The new test fails against the AI's version, which proves the point. The candidate then chooses the algorithm:

> **Candidate:** The classic fix is earliest deadline first. Sweep the slots in time order. Keep the orders that are already ready in a min-heap by deadline. Drop any whose deadline has passed, and give each slot's capacity to the most urgent orders. An exchange argument shows that's optimal for unit-size orders. I'll ask the AI to type it with a precise prompt.

The prompt names the signature, the sweep, the heap ordering, "copy the inputs, don't sort them in place", and the
target complexity. The output comes back, and the candidate reads it before pasting:

```java
while (!heap.isEmpty() && cap > 0) { ... }
heap.removeIf(o -> o.deadline() < slot.time());   // AI put this inside the slot loop
```

> **Candidate:** Logic's right, but `removeIf` scans the whole heap for every slot. That's O(n*m) hidden inside an O(log n)-looking loop. Expired orders always have the smallest deadlines, so they sit at the top of the heap. I'll replace it with a lazy pop: `while (!heap.isEmpty() && heap.peek().deadline() < t) heap.poll();`. Each order is then popped at most once.

All tests pass, including the counterexample.

**Phase 3: the large test.** It has 200,000 orders and 50,000 slots.

> **Candidate:** Sorting both lists is O(n log n + m log m), and each order enters and leaves the heap once, so O(n log n) total. That should be well under a second. Let me run it... 0.4 s, passing. One more edge case: a slot with capacity 0. The inner loop just skips it. Fine.

**Moments that earned points**

- Reading before prompting solved phase 1 in four minutes, and spotted a side effect for free.
- The candidate didn't accept AI code because it compiled. They **broke it with a counterexample test**, which is the clearest verification signal there is.
- The algorithm choice and its justification came from the candidate. The AI did the typing.
- The hidden `removeIf` was caught *in review*, before the big test exposed it, and the fix was explained in terms of the heap's invariant.
- Every prompt was announced and every output was checked out loud, so the interviewer never had to guess who was in control.
commonFailures: Prompting "solve this problem" and pasting the whole answer
Pasting code without reading it, then debugging the AI's mistakes under time pressure
Skipping orientation and spending 25 minutes on the phase-1 bug
Letting the model choose the algorithm, then failing the large hidden tests
Going silent while chatting with the AI, so the interviewer loses the thread
Not running tests after each change; stacking three unverified edits
Being unable to explain or simplify a generated block when asked
Refusing to use the AI at all, which wastes the round's main signal

rounds.title: Practical Coding (changing requirements + tests)
rounds.summary: Build a small, working component (rate limiter, TTL cache, job scheduler, webhook handler) in a real editor while the interviewer adds a requirement every 15-20 minutes. Tests are expected, and adapting cleanly to each change is the main signal.
whoRunsIt: Companies using CodeSignal's Industry Coding format
rounds.weight: ~15-20% where it replaces a DSA round; growing fastest of all formats
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 60-90 minutes.
- **Setup:** your own IDE, or CoderPad with a run button. Sometimes a starter repo with interfaces and a few tests. Internet docs are often allowed. AI is usually not (Stripe's integration round explicitly bans AI assistants).
- **Shape:** a progressive spec. Level 1 is the basic API. Each later level adds a twist: time windows, a second limit, capacity eviction, retries, cancellation, concurrency. CodeSignal's version runs 4 levels in about 90 minutes, and few people finish all four.
- **Atlassian's code-design round:** function signatures provided, the code must pass test cases, then a discussion of internals and of how you would improve usability and efficiency.
- **Typical prompts:** per-user + global rate limiter; TTL cache with max capacity; task scheduler with pause/retry/cancel; idempotent webhook receiver; booking without double booking; a small rules or discount engine; an in-memory key-value store with transactions; a bank ledger with scheduled transfers.
whatTheyTest: Turning a vague spec into a small, clear API with defined semantics
Getting a correct first version running fast, then improving it
Absorbing new requirements with small refactors instead of rewrites
Writing focused JUnit tests as you go, including boundary cases
Making time and randomness injectable so the code is testable
Thread-safety and failure semantics when the spec asks for them
Explaining trade-offs (accuracy vs memory, strictness vs simplicity)
rounds.rubric:
| Area | Strong hire | Hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|---|
| Progress | Reaches level 3-4; every finished level works | Reaches level 2-3, solid | Stuck on level 1, or later levels break earlier ones |
| Design | Small interfaces, logic separated from I/O, injectable clock | Reasonable structure, some coupling | God class, or a framework built up front for imagined needs |
| Change handling | Restates the new rule, finds the affected seam, refactors in minutes | Gets there with some patching | Rewrites from scratch or piles up `if` flags |
| Tests | Tests from level 1, reruns after each change, covers boundaries | A few tests, mostly happy path | None, or "I'd add tests later" |
| Communication | Names semantics and trade-offs before coding | Explains when asked | Silent, or can't justify choices |

Interviewers repeat one line in practical rounds: correctness and readability beat cleverness at every stage. A
boring level-3 solution with tests beats a brilliant, untested level-2 one.
rounds.howToAce:
**The playbook**

1. **Pin down semantics before code (3-5 min).** For a limiter: what does "100 per minute" mean, a fixed window or rolling? What does the caller get on rejection, a boolean or a retry-after? Per user, per key, global? Write the answers as comments at the top of the file. They become your test names.
2. **Write the interface first.** `boolean allow(String userId)` or `Optional<V> get(K key)`. Keep it tiny. Every later level should fit behind it.
3. **Inject time.** Pass a `LongSupplier nowMs` or a `java.time.Clock` into the constructor. Hard-coding `System.currentTimeMillis()` makes window, TTL and retry logic untestable, and interviewers notice.
4. **Simplest correct version, then a test immediately.** Have a JUnit 5 skeleton in your fingers: `@Test`, `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertThrows`. One happy-path test and one boundary test per level.
5. **When the requirement changes, follow a small loop.** Restate it ("so a user under their own limit can still be rejected by the global limit"). Name what breaks. Make the smallest refactor that creates a seam: extract a strategy, add a wrapper, split a method. Rerun all tests, add one new test.
6. **Separate the clock, the storage and the policy.** Most level-3 and level-4 twists change exactly one of them.
7. **Concurrency only when asked, but mention it early:** "Single-threaded for now. I'll make the per-key state atomic if we need concurrency." When it comes, use `ConcurrentHashMap.compute` or per-key locks, and say what's atomic and what isn't.
8. **Narrate trade-offs in one sentence each:** "A sliding log is exact but O(limit) memory per user. A token bucket is O(1) and allows controlled bursts."
9. **Manage the clock.** If a level takes more than 25 minutes, finish a simpler correct version, say what you'd improve, and move on.

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

Pick an LLD problem and write your own 4-level spec (for example: LRU cache, then TTL, then per-entry
weights, then thread-safety). Do it in 75 minutes in IntelliJ with JUnit. Repeat weekly with a different problem
from the list above.
commonFailures: Building a framework of interfaces and factories before anything runs
No tests, or tests only in the last five minutes
Hard-coded System.currentTimeMillis(), so time-based behaviour can't be tested
Rewriting from scratch at each new level instead of extending a seam
Ignoring semantics: inclusive vs exclusive boundaries, what happens on rejection
Not reading the provided starter code and tests before writing new code
Mixing console I/O and parsing into the core logic

rounds.title: Machine Coding / LLD
rounds.summary: India's signature product-company round: 90-120 minutes to build a working, extensible, in-memory system (BNPL wallet, cab booking, Splitwise) in your own IDE. A review follows where interviewers stress-test your code and add a requirement live.
rounds.weight: ~25% of the SDE-2 decision at Flipkart, PhonePe and Razorpay; usually an elimination round
rounds.format:
- **Coding:** 90-120 minutes on your own laptop in IntelliJ or similar, in person at Flipkart's offline drives. You get a problem document with **mandatory** and **bonus** requirements. No database, no UI: in-memory storage and a driver `main` or tests.
- **Review:** 30-90 minutes with one or two engineers. You walk through layers and patterns, they feed in edge cases ("this should never throw an unexpected exception"), you implement an extra strategy or a new requirement live, and sometimes draw a UML class diagram (Flipkart, Jan 2026).
- **Take-home variant:** PhonePe (Oct 2025) sent a 90-minute unproctored problem to email back, then held a 30-minute call on concurrency and design patterns.
- **Amazon-style LLD:** a 60-minute class-design discussion (Digital Wallet in a July 2025 SDE-2 loop) with less code and more modelling, plus two Leadership Principle questions.
- **Recent problems:** BNPL with credit limits and dues (Flipkart, 2026), phonebook (Flipkart), survey service and an in-memory blog search engine (Razorpay), customer-issue assignment (PhonePe), cab booking (Swiggy), plus classics like parking lot, Splitwise and elevator.
whatTheyTest: A working demo: the code runs end to end with a driver or tests
Entity modelling and clean layers (model, repository, service, strategy)
Extensibility: adding a new rule or strategy touches one or two classes
Edge cases and errors handled with clear custom exceptions
Concurrency awareness (two users booking the last seat)
Readable code: naming, small methods, no god class
Explaining and defending design choices in the review
rounds.rubric:
| Criterion | Strong hire | Hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runs | Demo works first time; driver covers every mandatory flow | Works with small fixes during review | Doesn't compile or crashes on the main flow |
| Requirements | All mandatory plus some bonus | All or nearly all mandatory | Major mandatory features missing |
| Modularity | Clear layers; services depend on interfaces | Mostly separated, a few leaks | Everything in `Main` or one service class |
| Extensibility | New requirement in the review lands in minutes, in one place | Lands with moderate edits | Needs rewiring across files, or `if-else` chains on type |
| Edge cases | Validation and custom exceptions; nothing unexpected escapes | Main edge cases covered | Raw `NullPointerException`s and `RuntimeException`s |
| Review | Explains trade-offs, admits shortcuts, knows the concurrency fix | Explains when probed | Can't justify the structure |

Working code is the gate. A beautifully layered design that doesn't run usually fails, while a slightly plain
design that runs and extends cleanly passes.
rounds.howToAce:
**The 90-minute plan**

1. **0-10 min: read, clarify, list.** Underline every noun (entities) and verb (operations). Ask what's mandatory and what's bonus, and confirm uniqueness rules, limits and what to show for invalid input. Write the operation list as comments in `Main`.
2. **10-20 min: skeleton.** Packages `model`, `repository`, `service`, `strategy`, `exception`. Models with fields and enums for states. Repositories as interfaces with an in-memory implementation backed by `ConcurrentHashMap` and `AtomicLong` ids.
3. **20-60 min: vertical slices.** Implement one mandatory operation end to end (service, repository, driver call), **run it**, then the next. Never have more than 15 minutes of unrun code.
4. **60-75 min: harden.** Validation, custom exceptions (`InsufficientCreditException`, `AgentUnavailableException`), and state-transition guards.
5. **75-85 min: bonus features,** chosen for value rather than ease.
6. **85-90 min: demo script.** The driver prints a readable story of the main flows and one or two failures. Delete dead code.

**Patterns: use the ones the problem asks for, no more**

- *Strategy* for anything that says "based on" (pricing, assignment, splitting, ranking).
- *State* (or an enum with guarded transitions) for lifecycles: order, ride, issue, booking.
- *Observer* for notifications.
- *Factory* when objects are created by type.
- *Singleton* only if asked. Prefer passing dependencies through constructors.

**Concurrency, in two sentences you can say in any review**

"Repositories use `ConcurrentHashMap`. Where a check-then-act decides a scarce resource (the last seat, a free
agent, the credit limit), I lock per entity or use a compare-and-set on the status, so two threads can't both
win."

**The review is half the score**

Expect "add X". Before answering, say *where* it plugs in: "That's a new `AssignmentStrategy` implementation and
one line in the factory." Then expect stress tests on invalid ids, double actions and empty states. Admit your
shortcuts plainly: "I skipped persistence of history; here's where it would go."

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

One problem a week from the LLD list, timed at 90 minutes in IntelliJ. Afterwards, give yourself an unseen
requirement (a bonus feature you invent) and time how long it takes to add. If it takes more than 15 minutes, the
design needs work.
rounds.walkthrough:
**Problem (original, similar in spirit to a 2025 PhonePe prompt):** build an in-memory customer-issue resolution
system. Mandatory: create an issue (transaction id, type such as PAYMENT or GOLD, subject, email); add agents with
expertise in issue types; assign an issue to an agent; an agent resolves an issue; view an agent's history; search
issues by email or type. Bonus: if no agent is free, put the issue on a waitlist and assign it when one frees up.

**Minute 0-8: clarify.**

> **Candidate:** Can an agent work on more than one issue at a time?
>
> **Interviewer:** One active issue at a time.
>
> **Candidate:** If several agents qualify, how do we choose? I'll make it pluggable. Default: the first free agent with that expertise.
>
> **Interviewer:** Fine.
>
> **Candidate:** Can a resolved issue be reopened?
>
> **Interviewer:** Out of scope.

**Minute 8-18: skeleton.** Entities: `Issue` (id, txnId, type, status, assignedAgentId), `Agent` (id, email,
expertise set, activeIssueId, history), and an `IssueStatus` enum with OPEN, ASSIGNED, RESOLVED and WAITING.
Interfaces `IssueRepository` and `AgentRepository` with in-memory implementations. `IssueService` handles create
and search, and `AssignmentService` handles assign, resolve and the waitlist.

```java
public interface AssignmentStrategy {
    Optional<Agent> pick(Issue issue, Collection<Agent> agents);
}

public final class FirstFreeAgentStrategy implements AssignmentStrategy {
    public Optional<Agent> pick(Issue issue, Collection<Agent> agents) {
        return agents.stream()
            .filter(a -> a.isFree() && a.handles(issue.getType()))
            .findFirst();
    }
}
```

**Minute 18-60: slices, each run immediately.** The candidate builds create-and-search first and runs it, then
assign and resolve, then history. The status transition lives in one guarded method on `Issue`:

```java
void markAssigned(String agentId) {
    if (status != IssueStatus.OPEN && status != IssueStatus.WAITING)
        throw new InvalidStateException(id, status, IssueStatus.ASSIGNED);
    this.status = IssueStatus.ASSIGNED;
    this.assignedAgentId = agentId;
}
```

**Minute 60-85: hardening and the bonus.** Unknown ids throw `NotFoundException`. Resolving an issue that isn't
assigned throws `InvalidStateException`. For the waitlist, an `EnumMap<IssueType, Deque<Issue>>` holds waiting
issues. When an agent resolves an issue, the service polls the first waiting issue matching that agent's
expertise. The driver prints the whole story, including two deliberate failures.

**The review.**

> **Interviewer:** New requirement: assign to the agent with the fewest resolved issues today, to balance load.
>
> **Candidate:** That's a new `AssignmentStrategy`. `LeastLoadedStrategy` filters the same way, then takes `min` by `resolvedToday()`. One new class plus the constructor argument in `Main`. The services don't change.

They write it in about six minutes and switch the driver over.

> **Interviewer:** Two requests call `assign` at the same moment and both see agent A as free. What happens?
>
> **Candidate:** With my current code, both could assign to A. That's a check-then-act race between `isFree()` and `markBusy()`. The smallest fix is to make the claim atomic on the agent: `activeIssueId` becomes an `AtomicReference<String>`, and claiming is `compareAndSet(null, issueId)`. If the CAS fails, the strategy tries the next candidate. The alternative is `synchronized` on the agent object. The CAS avoids holding a lock while I scan the other agents. In a real service with a database, it would be a conditional update: `UPDATE agent SET active_issue = ? WHERE id = ? AND active_issue IS NULL`, checking that one row changed.
>
> **Interviewer:** Why didn't you use a Singleton for the services?
>
> **Candidate:** Constructor injection keeps them testable and lets me swap the strategy. `Main` wires everything once, which gives one instance without the global state.

**Moments that earned points:** the clarifications changed the model (one active issue per agent). The code ran
after every slice, so the demo worked first time. The lifecycle sits in one guarded method instead of being
scattered. The new requirement took one class. The race was named precisely (check-then-act between `isFree` and
`markBusy`), fixed with the smallest correct primitive, and mapped to its database equivalent. Pattern questions
were answered with reasons, not pattern names.
commonFailures: Code that doesn't run at the end because everything was integrated in the last 10 minutes
Over-design: ten interfaces and five patterns for a 90-minute problem
A god service class, or all the logic in Main
if-else or switch on type where a strategy was obviously requested
No validation, so raw NullPointerExceptions escape during the review's edge-case tests
Chasing bonus features before every mandatory one works
Being unable to say where a new requirement would plug in
No answer when asked what happens if two threads do the same action

rounds.title: Concurrency Round
rounds.summary: Sometimes its own round, more often a 15-20 minute segment inside machine coding or a Java round: find the race, name the invariant it breaks, fix it in Java or SQL, and show how you'd test it.
rounds.weight: Often decides SDE-2 vs SDE-1 level at Java-heavy companies
rounds.format:
- **As a segment (most common):** inside a machine-coding review ("two requests assign the same agent"), a Java fundamentals round (`wait` vs `sleep`, `synchronized`, `volatile`), or a design round ("two workers pick the same job").
- **As a dedicated round (45-60 min):** implement something thread-safe (bounded blocking queue, rate limiter, LRU cache, a scheduler), or review a snippet and explain the race. Uber's SDE-2 machine coding explicitly covered asynchronous programming, thread synchronisation and parallel execution.
- **Database flavour:** conditional updates, optimistic locking with `@Version`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and `SKIP LOCKED` job claiming, isolation levels, deadlocks.
- **Modern Java:** `CompletableFuture` composition and timeouts; virtual threads (Java 21) and pinning, which JDK 24's JEP 491 largely removed for `synchronized`.
whatTheyTest: Naming race shapes precisely: check-then-act, read-modify-write, unsafe publication, lazy init
Choosing the smallest correct primitive (Atomic*, ConcurrentHashMap.compute, lock, semaphore, queue)
Knowing that a JVM lock does nothing across multiple service instances, and moving the guard to the DB or Redis
Database concurrency: isolation levels, row locks, optimistic vs pessimistic locking
Crash and retry semantics: leases, idempotency, at-least-once processing
Deadlock causes and prevention (lock ordering, timeouts)
Testing concurrent code with latches, thread pools and repeated runs
rounds.rubric:
| Signal | Strong hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnosis | Describes the exact interleaving: "T1 reads QUEUED, T2 reads QUEUED, both write RUNNING" | "There might be a race somewhere" |
| Invariant | States what must stay true: "a job has at most one active owner" | Talks about threads, not about correctness |
| Fix | Smallest correct scope, and right for the deployment (single JVM vs many instances) | `synchronized` on everything, or `volatile` on a counter |
| Trade-offs | Contention, lock hold time, throughput, failure modes | One answer, no alternatives |
| Failure thinking | Worker crash, retries, duplicate delivery, idempotency | Assumes nothing ever dies mid-operation |
| Proof | A concrete test: N threads, a latch, an assertion on the invariant | "I'd test it manually" |

The phrase interviewers listen for is a four-part answer: **the race, the broken invariant, the prevention, the
test.**
rounds.howToAce:
**Answer every concurrency question in four beats**

1. **Race:** the interleaving, step by step.
2. **Invariant:** what must always be true, in business terms.
3. **Prevention:** the primitive, its scope, and why it's enough.
4. **Proof:** how a test would fail before the fix and pass after.

**The race shapes to recognise on sight**

- *Check-then-act:* `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)`, `if (seat.isFree()) seat.book()`.
- *Read-modify-write:* `count++`, `balance = balance - amount`, an entity loaded, modified and saved.
- *Unsafe publication / lazy init:* double-checked locking without `volatile`, a shared `HashMap` or `SimpleDateFormat` in a singleton bean.
- *Lost update in the database:* two transactions read the same row and both write. The default REPEATABLE READ does **not** stop this for read-then-write code.

**Java toolbox you should be able to write from memory**

- `ConcurrentHashMap.merge` and `compute` for atomic per-key updates. `AtomicLong` and `LongAdder` for counters.
- A bounded blocking queue with `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s (`notFull`, `notEmpty`), using `while` loops around `await()`.
- `ExecutorService` plus `CountDownLatch` to release N threads at once in a test.
- `CompletableFuture.allOf(...)` with `orTimeout`, and `exceptionally` for fallbacks.
- Lock ordering (always lock the lower account id first) to prevent deadlock in transfers.

**Database toolbox (this is what makes it work across instances)**

- **Conditional update:** `UPDATE ... SET status='RUNNING' WHERE id=? AND status='QUEUED'`, then check that exactly one row changed.
- **Optimistic locking:** a `@Version` column. JPA adds `AND version=?` and throws on conflict, so you retry or reject.
- **Pessimistic locking:** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a short transaction. Add `SKIP LOCKED` (MySQL 8+) so workers grab different rows.
- **Unique constraints** as the last line of defence for idempotency (one refund per request id).

**Decide the scope out loud**

"Is this one JVM or several instances?" If several, a Java lock protects nothing and the guard must live in the
database, in Redis, or in a single-partition queue. Saying this early is a strong senior signal.

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

Work through the practical concurrency subject and the concurrency traps. Then take every LLD problem you've
solved and ask yourself: "Which operation decides a scarce resource, and what happens if two threads do it at
once?"
commonFailures: Adding synchronized to a service that runs on several instances
Using volatile for a counter (volatile gives visibility, not atomicity for count++)
containsKey then put on a ConcurrentHashMap, which is still a check-then-act race
Holding a lock or a DB transaction while calling a remote service
Assuming @Transactional or REPEATABLE READ prevents lost updates in read-modify-write code
Inconsistent lock ordering in transfers, leading to deadlock
Ignoring crashes and retries, so the fix still allows duplicate side effects
No test, or a single-threaded test that can't fail

rounds.title: Code Review Round
rounds.summary: You get a pull request or a file with planted bugs and design problems. You score by finding the issues that would break production first, then explaining impact and fixes like a reviewer people trust.
whoRunsIt: Meta (bug phase of the AI round)
Teams using HackerRank or CoderPad review tasks
rounds.weight: ~10-15% where it appears; growing because AI made writing code cheap and judging it valuable
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 30-60 minutes, sometimes as a segment of a coding or HM round.
- **Setup:** a diff view with inline comments (HackerRank's code-review question shows split or unified diffs, and the interviewer's rubric is hidden from you), or a file shared on screen. Usually 80-300 lines. For Raj's profile, expect Java with Spring Boot and JPA.
- **Variants:** "explain this code", then "what's wrong with it", then "fix the worst issue". Increasingly the code is AI-generated and looks clean: confident, idiomatic, subtly wrong.
- **Follow-ups:** "Are you sure that's a bug?", "Which one would you block the PR for?", "How would you phrase that comment to a junior?"
whatTheyTest: Reading unfamiliar code fast and stating its intent correctly
Ranking findings by production risk: correctness, data loss, security before style
Concrete impact and a concrete fix for each finding
Spring, JPA and Java pitfalls: transaction boundaries, N+1, thread-safety, resource leaks
Reviewing tests: what's missing, what's tested wrongly
Tone: separating blockers from nits, collaborating rather than lecturing
Holding a position under pushback when right, and updating when wrong
rounds.rubric:
| Signal | Strong hire | Hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prioritisation | Top 3 findings are the top 3 risks, called out first | Finds them, but mixed in with nits | Leads with formatting and naming |
| Depth | Explains the failure scenario ("two retries both refund") | Names the issue | "This looks off" |
| Fixes | Specific and proportionate | Generic ("add validation") | None, or "rewrite it" |
| Coverage | Correctness, security, failure handling, performance, tests | Two or three areas | Style only |
| Communication | Blocker vs nit labels; kind, precise wording | Clear | Harsh or vague |

Google's review guide orders concerns as design, functionality, complexity, tests, then naming, comments and
style, and says personal preferences should be marked "Nit:". Interview rubrics follow the same order.
rounds.howToAce:
**A fixed order of passes (about 25 minutes for 150 lines)**

1. **Intent (2 min).** Read the PR description, the method names and the tests. Say in one sentence what the code is meant to do. Many planted bugs are mismatches between intent and behaviour.
2. **Correctness and data integrity.** Business rules, boundaries, null and empty cases, money arithmetic, state transitions, idempotency, transaction boundaries, races.
3. **Security.** Injection (string-built SQL or JPQL), missing authorisation checks, secrets or personal data in logs, unvalidated input.
4. **Failure handling.** Swallowed exceptions, remote calls without timeouts, retries without backoff or idempotency, partial failure between the DB and an external call.
5. **Performance.** N+1 queries, `findAll()` then filtering in memory, unbounded caches and collections, work inside loops.
6. **Tests.** Is the risky path tested? Are the assertions meaningful?
7. **Design and readability.** Layering, naming, duplication. Mark these as nits unless they hide bugs.

**Comment template**

`[blocker] What: refund amount isn't checked against what was already refunded. Impact: repeated partial refunds can exceed the payment. Fix: check amount <= paid - refunded inside the same locked update.`

**Finish with a ranked summary:** "I'd block on 1-3, want 4-5 fixed before release, and 6+ are suggestions."

**The Spring and Java bugs that get planted most often**

- `@Transactional` on a private method, or called from the same class, so no proxy and no transaction.
- A remote HTTP call inside a DB transaction.
- `catch (Exception e)` that logs and returns success.
- `double` for money, `new BigDecimal(0.1)`, or `BigDecimal.equals` where scale differs.
- `equals` without `hashCode` on a class used as a map key or in a set.
- Shared mutable state in a singleton bean (`HashMap`, `SimpleDateFormat`).
- `Optional.get()` without a check. Streams or connections never closed.
- N+1 lazy loading in a loop. `findAll()` on a large table.
- Missing idempotency on a POST that moves money.
- `LocalDateTime` used for instants across time zones.

**When challenged**

Re-derive the bug from a concrete input instead of repeating yourself. If you were wrong, say so quickly. Updating
gracefully is itself a positive signal.

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

Use the testing and code review subject and the Spring and JPA traps as a bug catalogue. Then review real open
source PRs, or your own old code, out loud with a 25-minute timer, and write a ranked summary every time.
commonFailures: Opening with formatting, naming and missing comments
A flat list of 15 findings with no severity
Vague comments ("this could be better") without impact or fix
Missing the business-logic bug because only Java-level issues were checked
Not reading the tests, or not noticing that there are none
Proposing a full rewrite instead of targeted fixes
Folding immediately under pushback, or digging in without re-checking

rounds.title: Debugging & Production Incident Round
rounds.summary: Either fix a failing test in an unfamiliar repo (a "bug squash") or talk through a live incident such as "p99 latency tripled after the deploy". Either way you are scored on method: hypotheses, evidence, mitigation first, prevention after.
rounds.weight: ~10-20% where it's a round; incident questions also feed Ownership and Dive Deep signals in HM rounds
rounds.format:
**Flavour A: hands-on bug squash (45-60 min).** An unfamiliar repository with a failing test or an issue
description. Stripe lets you use your own IDE and language and look up docs and StackOverflow. A clear diagnosis
can count for more than a finished fix. AI is usually off.

**Flavour B: incident scenario (30-45 min, whiteboard).** The interviewer describes symptoms and reveals dashboards,
logs and recent changes only when you ask for them. Common scenarios: a regression after a deploy, one bad host or
shard, cache-driven DB overload, a cold cache after a restart, connection pool exhaustion, a retry storm.

**Flavour C: embedded.** "Tell me about the worst production issue you handled" in HM and behavioral rounds,
followed by a technical drill into it.
whatTheyTest: A systematic method instead of random poking
Asking for the right signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation, and what changed
Mitigating impact before chasing the root cause
Reading stack traces, logs, thread dumps and query plans
Knowing JVM, Spring and MySQL failure modes (pool exhaustion, GC, locks, slow queries)
Verifying the fix and adding guardrails so it doesn't recur
Calm, clear communication while under pressure
rounds.rubric:
| Signal | Strong hire | No hire |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | Confirms the symptom and scope: who, since when, how bad | Names a cause in the first 30 seconds |
| Evidence | Asks for golden signals, recent changes, healthy-vs-unhealthy comparison | Guesses, or asks for "all the logs" |
| Priorities | Mitigates first (rollback, flag off, shed load), then diagnoses | Debugs while users keep failing |
| Hypotheses | Ranked by likelihood and cost to test; each test can rule one out | Changes several things at once |
| Depth | Connects symptom to mechanism ("threads blocked on the pool because...") | Stops at "the DB was slow" |
| Closure | Verifies recovery, adds an alert, a test, a runbook, a postmortem | Stops once the graph goes green |

Google's SRE book makes the same point. In a major outage your first job is to make the system work, even before
you know why it broke, like a pilot who lands the plane before troubleshooting.
rounds.howToAce:
**The incident loop (say it, then walk it)**

1. **Confirm the symptom.** Which endpoints, users, regions? Since when? What's the error rate or latency versus the baseline?
2. **Check the four golden signals:** latency, traffic, errors, saturation. For each resource, check the **USE** method: utilisation, saturation, errors (CPU, memory, threads, DB connections, disk, network).
3. **Ask what changed:** deploys, config or feature flags, traffic pattern, dependency releases, data growth, certificate expiry.
4. **Compare healthy with unhealthy:** one host or all? One shard? One customer? One endpoint?
5. **Mitigate:** roll back, switch a flag off, scale out, shed or rate-limit load, fail over, drain a bad host.
6. **Verify** that the metrics recover and the symptom is gone for users.
7. **Find the root cause and add a guardrail:** a fix plus a regression test, an alert on the leading signal, a timeout or limit, and a blameless postmortem.

**The hands-on loop (bug squash)**

Reproduce by running the failing test. Read the assertion and the stack trace, starting from the first frame in
*your* code. Narrow down by bisecting inputs or commits, or by adding a log line. State a hypothesis, make the
minimal fix, add a regression test, and explain. Narrate what you've **ruled out**. That counts even if time runs
out.

**The Spring Boot and MySQL failure catalogue to know cold**

| Symptom | Likely mechanism | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `Connection is not available, request timed out` | Hikari pool exhausted by long transactions or slow queries | Pool active/pending metrics, thread dump |
| Latency grows with data size | Missing index or full scan, OFFSET pagination | Slow query log, `EXPLAIN` |
| Spike in queries per request after a release | New lazy relation causing N+1 | SQL logs, query count per request |
| Periodic latency spikes, rising memory | GC pressure, unbounded cache, leak | GC logs, heap dump |
| Everything slow when one dependency is slow | No timeout, thread pool saturated | Thread dump: threads in socket read |
| DB overload just after a cache flush | Cache stampede, no request coalescing | Cache hit ratio, DB QPS |
| Errors multiply during a partial outage | Retry storm without backoff or jitter | Request rate per client |
| Intermittent `Deadlock found` | Inconsistent lock order across transactions | `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` |

**Tools to name:** Spring Boot Actuator and Micrometer metrics, Prometheus and Grafana, structured logs with trace
ids, `jcmd` or `jstack` thread dumps, heap dumps, `EXPLAIN`, MySQL's slow query log and `performance_schema`.

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

Work through the production debugging and performance subjects. Then, once a week, pick one row from the
catalogue above and tell the incident story out loud from first page to postmortem, in under eight minutes.
rounds.walkthrough:
**Prompt:** "It's Tuesday evening. After this afternoon's deploy, checkout API p99 went from 300 ms to 4 s, and
about 5% of requests return 503 at peak. You're on call. Go."

> **Candidate:** First, scope. Is it only checkout, or every endpoint? All instances, or some? Did traffic change?
>
> **Interviewer:** Only the checkout endpoints. All six instances look the same. Traffic is a normal Tuesday peak.
>
> **Candidate:** All instances and normal traffic points away from a bad host or a load spike, and towards the deploy or a dependency. Saturation next: CPU, heap, Tomcat threads, DB pool, and what are the 503s actually saying?
>
> **Interviewer:** CPU is 30%. The heap looks normal. Tomcat busy threads are pinned at 200, the maximum. The logs show `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms`. DB CPU is moderate, about 40%.

> **Candidate:** So the app threads are all busy waiting for DB connections, but the database itself isn't struggling. That pattern usually means connections are being *held* too long, not that queries are slow. Something is keeping a connection checked out while it does other work. Before I dig in, though, I'd mitigate, because we're losing checkouts. The deploy correlates in time, and rolling back is cheap and reversible, so I'd roll back now and watch p99 and pool pending threads. If the change sits behind a feature flag, switching the flag off is even faster.
>
> **Interviewer:** You roll back. p99 returns to 320 ms within five minutes.
>
> **Candidate:** Good. That confirms the deploy and buys us time. Now the root cause. What changed in checkout in that release?
>
> **Interviewer:** The diff adds a call to a new fraud-scoring service from `CheckoutService.placeOrder`.
>
> **Candidate:** Is `placeOrder` annotated `@Transactional`, and where is the call?
>
> **Interviewer:** Yes, and the call is in the middle of the method, after the order insert.
>
> **Candidate:** That's the mechanism. The transaction opens at the start of `placeOrder` and takes a pool connection. The fraud call is an HTTP request. If its p99 is, say, 2-3 seconds, each checkout holds a DB connection for that long while doing no DB work. With a pool of 10 per instance, at peak we run out of connections. Requests queue for 30 seconds, then time out, and the 503s follow. Tomcat threads fill up waiting, which is why they're pinned at 200. To confirm in staging, a thread dump would show many threads in a socket read inside the fraud client, each holding a connection, and the rest waiting in `HikariPool.getConnection`. I'd also check the fraud client's timeout. I'd bet it's the default, which can be very long or infinite.
>
> **Interviewer:** How do you fix it?
>
> **Candidate:** Three layers. **The fix:** move the fraud call *before* the transaction starts, or split the work into a short transaction to create the order as PENDING, the fraud call with no transaction open, and a second short transaction to confirm or reject. **Resilience:** a strict timeout on the fraud client (say 500 ms) and a circuit breaker with an explicit fallback. Whether we fail open or fail closed is a business decision I'd confirm with the risk team. **Guardrails:** an alert on Hikari pending threads and on connection acquisition time, which would have fired minutes before the 503s. A load test in the pipeline for checkout. And a code review checklist item: no remote calls inside `@Transactional`. Then a blameless postmortem with the timeline.
>
> **Interviewer:** Would you just increase the pool size?
>
> **Candidate:** Not as the fix. A bigger pool only means more connections idling during HTTP calls, and six instances times a bigger pool can exceed MySQL's `max_connections` and hurt every other service. It might be a stop-gap if a rollback were impossible, but it treats the symptom.

**Moments that earned points:** scope first, which removed whole classes of causes. Saturation signals read
correctly (the app waiting on the pool while the DB is calm means connections held, not slow queries). Rollback
*before* root cause, with the reason it's safe. Specific evidence named for each hypothesis. The fix layered as
code, resilience and guardrails. And a confident, reasoned "no" to the tempting pool-size answer.
commonFailures: Naming a root cause before asking a single scoping question
Debugging while users keep failing, instead of rolling back or switching a flag off first
Never asking "what changed?"
Restarting servers as the whole answer
Reflexively increasing pool sizes, timeouts or instance counts
Stopping when the graph goes green: no verification, alert, test or postmortem
In hands-on rounds: editing code before reproducing the failure, or ignoring the stack trace

rounds.summary: 45-60 minutes designing a production system (payments, notifications, booking, delivery) from vague requirements to failure handling. It is now standard in SDE-2 loops and the biggest single signal for your level.
rounds.weight: ~25-30% of a senior decision; the main driver of SDE-1 vs SDE-2 levelling
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 45-60 minutes. Amazon's SDE-2 HLD round ran 1 hour 45 minutes in a July 2025 report because about 35 minutes of Leadership Principle questions were folded in. Flipkart combined it with the hiring manager round.
- **Tools:** a virtual whiteboard (Excalidraw, Whimsical, Miro) or a physical board in onsite drives. No code, though you may sketch an API or a table.
- **Prompts are production-flavoured:** subscription billing on top of a payment gateway (Razorpay), food delivery with four actor types (Amazon), an UrbanClap-style services marketplace (Flipkart), Twitter search (Walmart), monitoring tool (Goldman Sachs), plus the classics: URL shortener, notification system, ticket booking, chat.

whatTheyTest: Scoping: functional requirements, non-functional targets, and rough numbers
A clean API and data model, including keys and indexes
A high-level design that actually satisfies the requirements
Depth in two or three areas: consistency, idempotency, partitioning, caching, queues
Failure handling: timeouts, retries, dead letters, outbox, reconciliation
Trade-off reasoning tied to the requirements, not to buzzwords
Adapting calmly when the interviewer changes a constraint
rounds.rubric:
Hello Interview's levelling guidance matches what Indian SDE-2 loops ask for:

| | SDE-1 / mid-level | SDE-2 / senior (Raj's target) |
|---|---|---|
| Driving | Leads requirements, API and the high-level design; the interviewer drives the deep dives | Drives the whole session, picks the deep dives, and flags limits in their own design |
| Breadth | Knows what each box does and why it's there | Assumed; fundamentals are only probed if something sounds wrong |
| Depth | Textbook level | Experience-based detail in about two areas ("we hit this with MySQL locks when...") |
| Trade-offs | Names the options | Chooses, justifies with the requirements, and states the cost |
| Failure thinking | Mentions retries | Walks the failure paths: what happens when X is slow, down, or duplicated |

**No hire signals:** boxes before requirements, technology names that can't be explained, no data model, no
failure handling, designing Google scale for a small problem, and defending the design when the constraint changes.
rounds.howToAce:
**A time plan for 45-60 minutes** (adapted from Hello Interview's delivery framework)

1. **Requirements (5 min).** Three to five functional requirements, explicitly out-of-scope items, and non-functional targets: availability, latency, consistency, scale. Do back-of-envelope maths only where it changes a decision ("2M renewals on the 1st of the month is about 25/s spread over a day, but 500/s if we run it all in the first hour").
2. **Core entities (2 min)** and **API (5 min).** REST endpoints with request and response shapes. Put an **idempotency key** on anything that moves money or creates records.
3. **High-level design (10-15 min).** Draw the simplest design that satisfies the functional requirements, then walk one request through it end to end.
4. **Deep dives (15-20 min).** Pick the two or three hardest parts of *this* problem: usually correctness under retries and concurrency, the hot path's scaling, and failure handling. Raise them yourself: "The riskiest part here is double charging, so let me start with that."
5. **Wrap-up (3 min).** Observability (SLOs, key metrics, alerts), the biggest remaining risk, and what you would build next.

**Components every SDE-2 answer should include**

- Numbers: QPS (average and peak), storage growth, read/write ratio.
- A schema with primary keys, unique constraints and the indexes your queries need.
- A clear line between synchronous and asynchronous work, and why.
- A failure table: "If the gateway times out... if the worker crashes... if the queue is down..."
- The consistency choice for each piece of data (strong for balances, eventual for feeds).

**Topics to master, in priority order for 2027**

Caching patterns and invalidation; SQL schema design and indexing; replication and read replicas; partitioning
and sharding keys; queues, the outbox pattern and idempotent consumers; rate limiting; state machines for payments
and orders; observability and SLOs; then multi-region and cost as stretch topics.

**Use your own experience.** Raj has built Spring Boot and MySQL systems. Saying "in my current project, a
synchronous chain of three services caused cascading timeouts, so here I'd make step 2 asynchronous" is exactly the
experience-based depth the senior bar asks for.

**Practise on SwitchPrep**

One design a week, timed at 45 minutes, drawn in Excalidraw and explained out loud. Alternate between case
studies and the senior group (payments, idempotency, failure handling, job scheduler). After each one, write
the failure table from memory.
rounds.walkthrough:
**Prompt (original, similar in spirit to a Razorpay SDE-2 question):** "Design recurring subscriptions on top of
our existing one-time payment gateway. Merchants create plans (for example a monthly meal plan), customers
subscribe, and we charge them automatically every cycle until they cancel."

**Requirements.**

> **Candidate:** Functional: merchants create plans; customers subscribe with a saved payment mandate; we charge each cycle; we retry failed charges; customers can cancel; merchants get webhooks. Out of scope for now: proration, plan upgrades, and taxes. Is that the right cut?
>
> **Interviewer:** Yes.
>
> **Candidate:** Scale?
>
> **Interviewer:** Assume 2 million active subscriptions. Most renew on the 1st of the month.
>
> **Candidate:** So about 1.5 million charges land on one day. Spread over 12 hours, that's roughly 35 per second, but merchants will want them early in the day, so I'll design for a few hundred per second at peak and rate-limit ourselves towards the gateway and banks. The most important non-functional requirement is **never charge twice for the same cycle**. Next is never silently skipping a cycle. Latency barely matters: it's a batch.

**Entities and API.** Plan, Subscription (status ACTIVE, PAST_DUE, CANCELLED; `next_charge_at`), Invoice (one per
subscription per period), and PaymentAttempt (several per invoice). `POST /subscriptions` takes an
`Idempotency-Key` header. `POST /subscriptions/{id}/cancel`. Merchants receive webhooks for `invoice.paid` and
`invoice.failed`.

**High-level design.** A scheduler scans subscriptions whose `next_charge_at` is due, partitioned by id range so
several scheduler instances can share the work. It creates Invoices and publishes `charge-invoice` messages to a
queue. Charge workers call the gateway. A webhook receiver records asynchronous results from the gateway. A
notifier sends the merchant webhooks with retries.

**Deep dive 1: no double charges.**

> **Candidate:** Three layers. First, the Invoice has a unique key on `(subscription_id, period_start)`, so even if the scheduler runs twice, the second insert fails and no second invoice exists. Second, workers claim an attempt with a conditional update (`status` from PENDING to PROCESSING) and pass `invoice_id + attempt_no` as the idempotency key to the gateway, so a retried request can't create a second charge. Third, the queue is at-least-once, so the consumer is idempotent on that same claim.
>
> **Interviewer:** The gateway call times out. Did the customer get charged?
>
> **Candidate:** We don't know, and that's the dangerous case. I'd mark the attempt UNKNOWN, never blindly retry it, and query the gateway's status API with the same idempotency key, or wait for its webhook. A reconciliation job compares our UNKNOWN and PROCESSING attempts against the gateway's settlement report every hour. Only a confirmed failure moves to the retry schedule.

**Deep dive 2: the 1st-of-month spike.**

> **Candidate:** Pre-generate invoices the night before, so the scheduler isn't on the critical path. Charge workers pull from the queue with a concurrency cap per gateway and per bank, since banks throttle. Add jitter across the morning, and process merchants with earlier promised times first. If the gateway is degraded, a circuit breaker pauses the workers and the queue absorbs the backlog. Nothing is lost, only delayed.

**Deep dive 3: failed payments.** A dunning schedule retries after 1, 3 and 5 days at different times of day. After
the final failure, the subscription moves to PAST_DUE and the merchant gets a webhook. Every state change is an
event in an append-only `subscription_events` table, which helps with support questions and audits.

**Constraint change.**

> **Interviewer:** New regulation: customers must be notified 24 hours before every auto-debit, and can object.
>
> **Candidate:** That adds a state before charging: invoice created leads to NOTIFIED, and only after the 24-hour window does it become CHARGEABLE. The scheduler now runs two days ahead: it creates invoices and sends notices on day minus 1, and the charge workers only pick up CHARGEABLE invoices. Objections cancel the invoice. The good news is the rest of the design holds, because the invoice state machine was already the backbone.

**Observability.** SLOs on charge success rate per gateway and per bank, an alert on invoices stuck in UNKNOWN for
more than an hour, queue lag, and the reconciliation mismatch count, which should be zero.

**Moments that earned points:** the numbers changed the design (batch, not latency). The top non-functional
requirement was named and then designed for in three layers. The timeout question was answered with "we don't
know", followed by a safe procedure. The spike was handled with pre-generation and throttling. The constraint change
slotted in as one new state because the core abstraction was right. And observability was specific to this system,
not a generic "add monitoring".
commonFailures: Drawing boxes before agreeing on requirements and scale
No numbers at all, so no decision is justified
Buzzword soup: Kafka, CQRS, sharding and microservices with no reason tied to the problem
No data model, or tables without keys and indexes
Only the happy path: nothing on timeouts, retries, duplicates or crashes
Designing global scale for a modest problem
Waiting for the interviewer to drive the deep dives
Defending the original design when a constraint changes instead of adapting it

rounds.title: Resume Deep Dive (your own stack)
rounds.summary: 45-60 minutes where an engineer picks lines from your resume (Spring Boot, JPA, MySQL, Angular) and keeps asking "why?" and "how does that work underneath?" until they find the edge of your knowledge. It can't be bluffed.
rounds.weight: ~20-25% of the decision at Java-heavy companies; often the first technical round
rounds.format:
- **Duration:** 45-80 minutes. Walmart's SDE-3 round 1 ran 80 minutes and covered projects, Java Streams coding, Java 8 interface rules, collections, Spring DI and bean scopes, Hibernate mapping, an SQL query without subqueries, a REST endpoint, and AWS IAM, because it was on the resume.
